title: #409 From Product to Innovation: Mike Todasco on AI, Automation, and the Future of Technology

turns.speaker: Announcer
paragraphs: From the heart of Dubai where tomorrow is being built today to the world. Welcome to the CTO show with Mehmet. Here we redefine technology and reimagine possibilities. With Mehmet, delve into the riveting realms of AI, cybersecurity, and digital technology. Experience the thrilling highs and lows of startups. Immerse yourself in the spirit of entrepreneurship and witness the future of business innovation being written in real time. Now, without further ado, let's tune in and explore the future.

paragraphs: I want to get back to two examples. The first one kind of went exceeded our expectations. The first the second one did not. We had a really a brilliant engineer who was kind of doing this as a side project.

He was looking at the new Bluetooth 4.0 specs that were coming out. Kind of came to the realization that, huh, this little, you know, we could take a little piece of hardware as represented by the pen here and this could actually talk to a mobile device. Like if you have hardware that's in a retailer store talking with the mobile device that the customer has on their person, well, what can you do in those circumstances?

So it was super exciting building that out. And that was a circumstance where the merchants, the retailers, they loved it. I mean, I will say we talked to a very large coffee retailer for one. And that coffee retailer was like, well, does this mean that if somebody pulls up in the parking lot that this little device can actually know that this person has actually pulled up and is talking to that passively and we could start making their coffee the second they pull in because we know what their favorite is or whatever. Like yeah, that's the kind of stuff that you could do here. So I don't think there was a large retailer in America, potentially the world that we were talking to about this product.

The flip side of that is consumers hated it. And it's not for the reasons that you would think that they would hate it today. So we actually had so where PayPal's headquarters is in San Jose, right up the highway 101 is Palo Alto, which is where Stanford University is headquartered. And they're just like, why? I have a credit card. I don't need that. And look, these were as tech savvy as you could possibly be. But in 2013 it was not the right. And look, here's the reality. Merchants loved it. Consumers did not love it. They just did not see the use of that.

And this was a great way. We tried some tweaks to the product, we tried to do some value add. Like, you know, you can only do so many offers and a new payment product because the margins and payments, you know, like if somebody spends $10, like 30 cents of that is going to PayPal roughly. There just wasn't the energy within the company to like create this entirely new business because we're frankly too early. So that was a time where I mean, and thank goodness we did talk to customers and did do this small sample because the world really wasn't ready for it.

turns.speaker: Mehmet Gonullu
paragraphs: And now like further like I mean beside or let's say putting, you know, what you've done at PayPal aside, I want you know, Mike in general like because you run, you know, the innovation lab over there, right? turns.speaker: Mike Todasco
paragraphs: And I would say for starters, the first thing I would ask if you're looking to start an innovation lab, like it is what you're alluding to here is like what's the goal? Like why are you doing this? Are you doing this because you want to tell shareholders or employees that you're doing innovative stuff? I mean, maybe that's it. Maybe that is a good reason to just say like, hey, yeah, we got we got innovation, we're checking a box there. Is there some competitive threats in the short, medium or long term that you think you're facing? Are there other things that are happening where, you know, you just need that or you need to build up the culture and work these muscles or whatever it might be?

Like I think the first step in it is to prospectively see what it is that you're actually trying to achieve. Then what I would actually do with that alongside, I would then kind of take a look at the I think this was McKinsey put out like the innovation horizons. There's like horizon one innovation, horizon two and horizon three. And horizon one is like and again, none of the this is not said disparagingly for horizon one specifically, but like it's incremental innovation. It's existing products, existing markets, but improving, constant improvements, you know, just like how are you building out better, kind of what's going on in the next six to 12 months almost.

Horizon two would be like new technologies for existing customers or existing technologies for new customers. That would be that. And that's a lot of what we focused on at the innovation lab at PayPal was horizon two. Horizon three is also going way further out there. That is much more like new technologies, new markets done in a completely different way, different time frame. This is Microsoft research, you know, or Bell Labs. This is looking at quantum computing. This is this is much further out there. We strategically said we were not going to be playing in that game. The focus was going to be on horizon two innovation.

So once you sort of have that defined, the next thing I would say and look, just because you define it now also doesn't mean that it can't change. One of the things about innovation is like you need to be flexible. For us at PayPal, the focus was really it really wasn't about the products as much as permeating the innovation culture that we had as a company that really was at the company's core from its starting. There's so many, you know, both little and big innovations that just came out of necessity from the very early days at PayPal. A guy named Jimmy Sony wrote a book recently called The Founders that kind of walks through a lot of that.

How do you make that work for 20,000, 30,000 people? And so a lot of that was the focus that we had at the company just within PayPal. And the last step that I will actually give on that was do it with not much money. Start low.

I'm like, hey, what's what's Todasco doing over there? Because we had no money. turns.speaker: Mehmet Gonullu
